blocks.p: Midea's U-shaped inverter unit changed what people expect from a window air conditioner. The body is split into an indoor and an outdoor half joined by a channel, and the lower window sash closes down into that channel. That puts the compressor outside the window and lets the sash itself block much of the noise, which is why Midea markets it as one of the quietest window units available. The inverter compressor is the other half of the story: rather than cycling fully on and off, it slows down once the room is near the setpoint, which saves energy and avoids the clunk-and-roar of a fixed-speed unit starting every few minutes. Midea rates the 8,000 BTU model for rooms of up to about 350 square feet, and it carries Energy Star certification. It is bulkier than the 5,000 BTU picks and suits double-hung windows only. For a bedroom where you want to sleep with the AC running, it is the one to buy.

sections.h: BTU per Square Foot: Sizing a Small Window AC

blocks.p: The most common mistake with a small window AC is buying by price and hoping it is big enough. Energy Star's sizing guidance is the right starting point: about 5,000 BTU for 100 to 150 square feet, 6,000 BTU for 150 to 250, 7,000 BTU for 250 to 300, and 8,000 BTU for 300 to 350 square feet. Measure the room's length and width, multiply, and start there.

Then adjust. Energy Star suggests adding about 10 percent for a very sunny room and reducing by about 10 percent for a heavily shaded one. Add roughly 600 BTU for each person beyond two who regularly uses the room, and add around 4,000 BTU if the unit is cooling a kitchen. A top-floor bedroom under an uninsulated roof, or a home office full of computers, behaves like a bigger room than its floor area suggests.

Oversizing is not free insurance. A unit that is too big cools the air quickly and shuts off before it has run long enough to pull moisture out, leaving the room cold and clammy. That matters in humid climates, where dehumidification is half of what makes a room comfortable. If damp air is the real problem, especially below grade, a dedicated dehumidifier from our [best basement dehumidifier](/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) guide may be the better buy. Inverter units are more forgiving of oversizing because they slow down instead of shutting off.

For most small bedrooms, a 5,000 BTU unit is enough. If the room is between 150 and 250 square feet, or gets afternoon sun, a 6,000 BTU unit like the LG LW6017R is the safer choice. Above that, the 8,000 BTU Midea U-shaped inverter covers rooms up to about 350 square feet, and it does so more quietly than any fixed-speed unit.

blocks.p: The six picks below are all 115-volt units that plug into a standard household outlet. Room coverage figures come from manufacturer listings and are best read alongside the sizing guidance above, not as a guarantee for every room.

The biggest split is the compressor. Five of the six use a conventional fixed-speed compressor that is either fully on or off, which is cheap, simple and loud. The Midea U-shaped unit uses an inverter compressor that varies its speed, which is the single biggest improvement in window air conditioning in years, for both efficiency and noise.

The second split is window type. All but one need a standard double-hung window that opens vertically. If your windows slide sideways or crank outward, skip straight to the Frigidaire FFRS0822SE or read the narrow-window section below before buying anything else.

Every window AC lists a minimum and maximum window width and a minimum opening height. Check both against your window before you order, and measure the actual clear opening with the sash raised, not the window frame. Many small 5,000 BTU units fit windows from the low twenties up to the mid-thirties in inches, but the exact range varies by model, so read the spec sheet for the one you are buying rather than assuming.

A truly narrow window AC is a different product. Horizontal slider windows open sideways and leave a tall, thin gap, which a standard box unit cannot fill. Slider and casement units like the Frigidaire FFRS0822SE are built tall and narrow for exactly that opening. Casement windows, which crank outward, usually need a filler panel cut from rigid material to close the gap around the unit, and the window may have to be removed or the crank mechanism worked around. If that sounds like more than you want to take on, a handyman can do it in an hour or two.

If the window simply will not take any window unit, a portable AC is the fallback, but go in with open eyes. Portables sit in the room and push hot air out through a hose, and single-hose models also pull replacement air in from around doors and windows. That makes them noticeably less efficient than a window unit of the same BTU rating. Buying a used portable AC can make sense on a budget, but test it before money changes hands, check the hose and window kit are included, and avoid units that have been stored on their side.

For mobile homes, older apartments and sunrooms with odd openings, a through-the-wall unit or a ductless mini-split may be worth considering. Both need more installation work, and a mini-split needs a licensed HVAC contractor and usually a dedicated circuit, but they solve the window problem permanently.

sections.h: Inverter vs Fixed-Speed: Efficiency and Noise

blocks.p: A conventional window AC runs its compressor at full speed until the room hits the thermostat setting, then shuts it off completely. When the room warms a degree or two, the compressor starts again with a thump and a roar. That cycle repeats all night, and it is the main reason small window units have a reputation for being hard to sleep next to.

An inverter compressor varies its speed. Once the room is close to the setpoint, it slows down and keeps running quietly rather than stopping and restarting. The result is steadier temperature, less noise, better dehumidification because the coil stays cold, and lower energy use. Manufacturers' Energy Star listings show inverter window units reaching much higher efficiency ratings than typical fixed-speed units of the same size.

Midea's U-shaped design adds a second noise advantage. Because the window sash closes down into a channel between the indoor and outdoor halves, the compressor sits outside the glass and the sash blocks much of the sound. Owners commonly report it as dramatically quieter than a conventional box unit, which is why it is our top pick for bedrooms.

Is an inverter worth the extra money? For a bedroom you sleep in all summer, yes. For a guest room used a few nights a year, a garage workshop or a dorm, a basic fixed-speed 5,000 BTU unit does the job at a fraction of the price. The inverter pays back fastest where the unit runs many hours a day and where noise matters.

sections.h: CEER and What It Costs to Run

blocks.p: CEER stands for Combined Energy Efficiency Ratio, and it is the efficiency number on the yellow EnergyGuide label for room air conditioners sold in the US. It is the cooling output in BTU per hour divided by the power used, including the small amount the unit draws in standby. A higher CEER means more cooling per watt. It replaced the older EER rating, so compare like with like when reading older reviews.

Most basic 5,000 BTU fixed-speed units sit at the lower end of the CEER range, while inverter units sit well above it. Check the EnergyGuide label or the Energy Star listing for the exact model you are considering, because the number can differ between model years even under the same name.

To estimate running cost, find the unit's rated wattage on its label or in the manual, multiply by the hours it runs, and multiply by your electricity rate. A 5,000 BTU unit typically draws somewhere around 400 to 500 watts while its compressor runs, and an 8,000 BTU unit more. Running eight hours a night for a summer adds up to a noticeable but modest amount on most bills, and an inverter unit trims it further by running slower most of the night.

A home energy monitor, like those in our best home energy monitor guide, shows exactly what a window unit adds to your bill. That is useful if you are deciding whether an inverter upgrade will pay for itself, or whether cooling one room with a window unit beats running central air for the whole house overnight.

sections.h: Running Watts, Starting Surge, Generators and Power Stations

blocks.p: A window AC has two power numbers that matter off-grid. Running watts are what it draws once the compressor is going, typically around 400 to 500 watts for a 5,000 BTU unit and more for 6,000 and 8,000 BTU units. Starting watts are the brief surge when a fixed-speed compressor kicks on, which can be two to three times the running figure for a fraction of a second. That surge happens every time the compressor cycles, not just when you switch the unit on.

On a generator, a 5,000 or 6,000 BTU unit is an easy load for a 2,000-watt-class inverter generator, and many people run one through a heat wave during an outage. Generators must run outdoors only, never in a garage, basement, shed or porch, and well away from windows, doors and vents, with working carbon monoxide alarms inside the home. Run the AC from a heavy-duty outdoor-rated extension cord to the generator, never by backfeeding a household outlet. For whole-home coverage, a transfer switch installed by a licensed electrician is the safe route; our [best home generator for power outages](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/) guide covers sizing and connection.

On a portable power station, the maths is less forgiving. The station's inverter must handle the running watts continuously and the compressor's starting surge, and the battery drains quickly. As a rough guide, a 1,000 watt-hour station running a 5,000 BTU unit with its compressor running most of the time lasts on the order of a couple of hours, less on a hot afternoon. Inverter AC units help here because they soft-start and run slower once the room cools, but no small station will run a window AC all night.

If you want to cool a bedroom through an outage on battery, a larger home backup battery or a power station with solar input is the realistic path, and a small fixed-speed unit sized exactly to the room is easier to support than a big one. Our [best portable power station](/best-portable-power-station/) guide lists continuous and surge ratings for each station. For lighter needs, a fan from our [best battery-powered fan](/best-battery-powered-fan/) guide runs for many hours on the same energy.
SAFETY
Generators outside, cords rated for the load, no backfeeding.

Carbon monoxide from a generator kills people every year during heat waves and outages. Keep it outdoors and well away from openings, run cords rather than connecting to house wiring, and have a licensed electrician install a transfer switch for anything more.

sections.h: Window ACs in Campers, Sheds and Tents

blocks.p: People do fit small window ACs into pop-up campers, teardrops, cargo-trailer conversions and sheds, and a 5,000 BTU unit is often enough for a small, well-shaded space. It can be a cheap, effective alternative to a dedicated RV air conditioner, with some important caveats.

A household window unit is not built for the road. Vibration while towing can damage the compressor mounts and refrigerant lines, so treat it as a parked-only setup: remove it or support it properly before travel, and never rely on a household AC's window brackets to hold it in a moving trailer. The opening needs a weather-tight frame, the unit must tilt slightly outward so condensate drains outside, and the surrounding wall has to bear the weight.

Power is the next limit. At a campground, a 5,000 or 6,000 BTU unit runs comfortably on a 15-amp or 30-amp pedestal, as long as you are not also running a microwave and a space heater on the same circuit. Use correctly rated adapters, never cheater plugs that drop the ground; our best RV power adapter guide covers the safe ones. Off-grid, the generator and power station limits above apply, and a generator must stay well away from the camper's windows and vents.

For tents and vans, a purpose-built portable unit is usually the better choice. Our best portable air conditioner for camping guide covers units designed for those spaces, including some that run directly from 12V. A window AC in a tent needs a homemade box and an insulated, sealed tent to be worth the effort.

sections.h: Installing It Safely, and Buying on Amazon

blocks.p: Window AC units are heavy and sit above people's heads, so installation deserves care. Use the brackets and screws supplied, add an exterior support bracket if the manufacturer recommends one or if the unit sits above a walkway, and secure the sash so it cannot be raised from outside. Many units must tilt slightly toward the outside so condensate drains away from the house; follow the manual's angle rather than guessing. Two people make the lift much safer, even for a 5,000 BTU unit.

Plug the AC directly into a properly grounded wall outlet. Most manufacturers say not to use an extension cord or power strip, and the plug on many units includes a built-in leakage-current detector for that reason. Larger units can trip a breaker shared with other loads; if the circuit trips repeatedly, have a licensed electrician check whether the room needs a dedicated circuit. Do not replace a breaker with a larger one to stop it tripping.

Buying a window AC on Amazon is fine, and the prices are often good, but inspect the box and unit on arrival. Look for dents, bent fins and oil stains, and keep the packaging until you have run it for a few days. Many manufacturers recommend letting a unit stand upright for some hours before first use if it may have been shipped on its side, so the compressor oil settles; check the manual for the exact time.

Before summer, clean or rinse the filter, check that the exterior fins are clear of debris and that the unit drains properly. A filter clogged with dust reduces airflow and cooling and makes the coil more prone to freezing. At the end of the season, either remove the unit and store it upright or cover the outside with a breathable cover rated for it.

Buy the **Midea U-Shaped 8,000 BTU Inverter** if the unit goes in a bedroom you sleep in, or anywhere noise and running cost matter. It is the best small window air conditioner for most people with a double-hung window and a room up to about 350 square feet, and the inverter also makes it the easiest of these to run from a power station.

Buy the **LG LW6017R** if your room is between 150 and 250 square feet, or a 5,000 BTU unit would struggle with afternoon sun, and you want a remote and timer at a modest price. Buy the **Midea EasyCool**, **Frigidaire FFRA051WAE** or **BLACK+DECKER BD05MWT6** for a small room on a tight budget; choose between them on price, availability and window fit.
Buy the **Frigidaire FFRS0822SE** if your windows slide sideways or crank outward. It costs more than a box unit, but it is far more efficient than settling for a portable AC.

For a camper, any of the 5,000 BTU mechanical units are the easiest to support on shore power or a generator, as a parked-only setup. And if you need cooling through power outages, buy the AC sized exactly to the room, pair it with a generator or a large battery system, and keep fans in reserve for when the battery runs low.

mistakes: Buying by price instead of room size

A 5,000 BTU unit in a sunny 220 square foot room will run flat out and never catch up. Measure the room, use Energy Star's sizing ranges, and adjust for sun, occupants and kitchens. A slightly bigger unit, or an inverter that slows down, beats one that is too small for the heat load.

Every window AC has a minimum and maximum window width and a minimum opening height. Measure the clear opening with the sash raised before ordering. Slider and casement windows need a purpose-built unit, and discovering that after a heavy unit arrives means a return shipment and a hot week.
Running the AC on an extension cord or power strip

Most manufacturers say to plug a window AC directly into a grounded wall outlet. Household extension cords and power strips can overheat under a compressor load. If the breaker keeps tripping, have a licensed electrician check whether the room needs a dedicated circuit rather than upsizing the breaker.
Running a generator too close to the house

A generator powering an AC during a heat wave must run outdoors, well away from windows, doors and vents, never in a garage or on a porch. Carbon monoxide is invisible and deadly. Run an outdoor-rated cord to the AC and keep working CO alarms inside.
Expecting a power station to run it all night

A 5,000 BTU unit draws hundreds of watts while its compressor runs, plus a starting surge each cycle. A 1,000 watt-hour station lasts on the order of a couple of hours. Plan for a generator, a much larger battery system, or fans once the station runs low.
bottomLine: For most bedrooms, the Midea U-Shaped 8,000 BTU Inverter is the best small window air conditioner: quiet enough to sleep beside, efficient, and gentle on a generator or power station. For a small room on a budget, any of the 5,000 BTU mechanical units will do the job, and the LG LW6017R is the step up for rooms that need 6,000 BTU. If your windows slide or crank open, buy the Frigidaire FFRS0822SE rather than settling for a portable. And whatever you buy, measure the room and the window first, plug it straight into the wall, and keep any generator outdoors and well away from the house.

faqs.q: What size window AC do I need for a small bedroom?
faqs.a: Energy Star suggests 5,000 BTU for 100 to 150 square feet and 6,000 BTU for 150 to 250. Add about 10 percent for a very sunny room and reduce it for a shaded one. Most small bedrooms need 5,000 BTU, but a top-floor room or one with afternoon sun often does better with 6,000 BTU.

faqs.q: What is the best narrow window AC?
faqs.a: For horizontal slider or casement windows, the Frigidaire FFRS0822SE is built specifically for that tall, narrow opening and is widely available. A standard box unit will not fit a slider. If no window unit will fit at all, a portable AC is the fallback, but it is noticeably less efficient than a window unit of the same rating.

faqs.q: Is an inverter window AC worth it?
faqs.a: For a bedroom you sleep in all summer, yes. An inverter compressor slows down instead of cycling on and off, so it is quieter, holds a steadier temperature, removes more humidity and uses less energy. For a guest room, garage or dorm used occasionally, a basic fixed-speed 5,000 BTU unit is the better value.

faqs.q: Can I run a small window AC on a generator?
faqs.a: Yes. A 5,000 or 6,000 BTU unit is an easy load for a 2,000-watt-class inverter generator. Run the generator outdoors only, away from windows, doors and vents, with CO alarms inside. Connect the AC with an outdoor-rated extension cord and never backfeed the house; a licensed electrician should install a transfer switch for anything more.

faqs.q: How long will a power station run a window AC?
faqs.a: Not long. A 5,000 BTU unit draws roughly 400 to 500 watts while the compressor runs, so a 1,000 watt-hour station lasts on the order of a couple of hours, less in the heat. The station also needs enough surge capacity for the compressor start. Inverter units help, but overnight cooling needs a much larger battery system or a generator.

faqs.q: Can I put a window AC in a camper?
faqs.a: Many owners fit a 5,000 BTU unit in a pop-up, teardrop or trailer conversion, but treat it as a parked-only setup. Household units are not built for towing vibration, so remove or properly support them before travel. Build a weather-tight frame, let it drain outside, and run it on shore power or a generator kept well away from the camper.

faqs.q: Is it safe to buy a window AC on Amazon?
faqs.a: Yes, from the brand or a reputable seller. Inspect the unit on arrival for dents, bent fins and oil stains, and keep the packaging until it has run for a few days. If it may have shipped on its side, let it stand upright for the time the manual recommends before first use so the compressor oil can settle.
